rationale: Numbered presentations include pressure measurements during saliva swallows and binary drooling in a retrospective Parkinson sample. The collection supplies no raw-fig exposure. The 13 gaps in published numbering are recorded.
A clinical review of postinjury disorders of consciousness mentions drooling among medication adverse effects. Neither population nor exposure matches the frozen claim.
The differential diagnosis review describes drooling as a possible bulbar feature of early-onset parkinsonism and other disorders. It contains no measured effect of raw fig.

Early Parkinson clinical interviews distinguish spontaneous and prompted reports of drooling. The original figure reports seven spontaneous and six prompted accounts. It supplies symptom presence and no change after eating raw fig.
The trial reports sialorrhea or salivary hypersecretion in antipsychotic safety monitoring in adolescents. The evaluated exposure and population differ from the claim.
The gut–brain workshop summarizes drooling frequencies from five earlier surveys using different instruments. The table does not measure raw fig, and its entries represent separate cited cohorts.
The validated form groups salivation with other nonmotor symptoms in one frequency item. The original supplement supplies no isolated drooling-severity or raw-fig estimate.
This series concerns medication-associated hypersalivation in psychiatric care. Its treatment, underlying population and outcome context differ from the claim.

An observational analysis within STEADY-PD III reports more new endorsement of the saliva and drooling item among people starting symptomatic treatment in year two. The analysis concerns symptom emergence rather than severity change and contains no raw-fig comparison.
The geriatric swallowing practice report treats drooling as a clinical observation during assessment. It is an expert recommendation and contains no raw-fig Parkinson trial.
The diagnostic review discusses drooling and swallowing signs when considering parkinsonian syndromes. It does not measure a food-related change.
The clinical literature review examines parkinsonism reported in the setting of another illness. It supplies no raw-fig or Parkinson drooling comparison.
The review considers proposed disease associations with infection and commensal communities. It supplies no raw-fig intervention or graded drooling outcome.
The guideline catalogs drug-related sialorrhea in schizophrenia care. It provides no original clinical comparison for raw fig or Parkinson drooling.
The review concerns stimulation treatments and motor outcomes. Drooling appears as a Parkinson clinical feature, without a measured fig exposure.
The clinical case-report review concerns pediatric illness. It does not supply a Parkinson or raw-fig drooling comparison.
The multisystem Parkinson review discusses severe sialorrhea and saliva samples while describing different clinical pathways. It contains no tested culinary exposure for the outcome.
The review classifies complex childhood-onset movement disorders. Its populations, exposures and clinical scope do not match the raw-fig Parkinson claim.

The registry reports 172 drooling endorsements among 365 questionnaire respondents with reported multiple system atrophy. The survey gives symptom presence in a distinct diagnosis and no raw-fig comparison.
The family case series concerns a distinct paroxysmal movement disorder. It contains no tested raw-fig exposure with measured Parkinson drooling severity.
This review describes sialorrhea and dysphagia among gastrointestinal features of Lewy body disorders. It provides no fig-specific dietary endpoint or measured raw-fig effect.
The Parkinson model study evaluates a cell therapy in animals. Its experimental intervention and endpoints provide no human food or graded drooling comparison.
The ALS case records absent drooling in the clinical history and studies a different diagnosis. It has no raw-fig exposure comparison.
The clinical review covers movement disorder reports around another illness. It supplies no measured culinary fig exposure and Parkinson drooling comparison.
